title: Building Societal Resilience: Willingness to Defend, Financial and Institutional Resilience in Estonia and Lithuania
content: Research on societal resilience and national security has increasingly focused on the factors that determine citizens’ readiness to defend the state; however, the interrelationships among individual financial resilience, institutional trust, and motivation for civil defense remain under-explored. The aim of this article is to empirically assess the direct and indirect effects of individual financial resilience on citizens’ willingness to defend the state, and to compare the structure of these relationships in Estonia and Lithuania, while accounting for the moderating effects of income and ethnicity. The study employed a quantitative comparative research method, and moderated mediation was applied to assess to hypothesis. The results showed that in both countries, individual financial resilience significantly increases institutional trust and citizens’ willingness to defend the state, and that institutional trust significantly mediates this relationship. In Estonia, a significant moderating effect of income and ethnic affiliation was found, whereas in Lithuania, the influence of these factors was not confirmed. The results indicate that financial resilience and institutional trust are important prerequisites for public willingness to defend the country, but their interaction depends on the national context. This study contributes to research on societal resilience and national security by highlighting the importance of economic and institutional factors in shaping citizens’ willingness to contribute to national defense.
